rule.rule_text: Dialogue stays verbatim: copy the script byte-for-byte. Do not reword, translate, add, drop, or 'correct' grammar unless the director explicitly approves that change.
rule.rationale: Rewritten lines break lip-sync targets and legal/script lock. Directors treat the script as the source of truth.
rule.good_example: The script line is kept exactly, including punctuation and the original wording, and only that speaker's mouth moves on that line.
rule.bad_example: A typo in the script is silently 'fixed', or the line is translated into another script, or extra words are added for clarity.

rule.rule_text: Never change shot types, shot order, shot count, framing, or durations unless the director asks for that exact change.
rule.rationale: Extra cuts and unplanned close-ups break pacing and hide locked group blocking.
rule.good_example: An approved 2-shot clip keeps exactly two shots and one cut at the scripted time; camera moves stay as written.
rule.bad_example: A 2-shot prompt is rendered as three shots because an unscripted close-up insert is added in the middle.

rule.rule_text: Any readable on-screen writing must use only the language script required by the show's rules. For Hindi shows in this pipeline, visible text is Hindi Devanagari only. Dialogue may be stored in the prompt in the form the current episode lock specifies (Devanagari or Roman), but it is still verbatim.
rule.rationale: Shows have used both Devanagari-only and Roman-Hindi dialogue locks on different episodes; follow the current episode lock, and never invent a new wording.
rule.good_example: Banners, decrees and carved inscriptions are written in the required script and match the locked wording.
rule.bad_example: A sign, scroll or banner appears in the wrong alphabet, or the prompt changes the written words.

rule.rule_text: Every character who appears gets a Positions line: screen side, depth, posture, movement and facing. Sides stay locked from shot to shot and from the previous track's end state unless the story moves them on camera.
rule.rationale: Mirrored blocking and dropped characters are a repeated failure mode.
rule.good_example: The previous track ended with A at screen-left and B at screen-right; the next track opens on those same sides and names both people in every shot.
rule.bad_example: A wide shot mirrors the pair so A is suddenly screen-right, or a character who should be present is simply omitted.

rule.rule_text: Name every character in every shot with position, posture, movement and facing. Never use a group shorthand such as 'the brothers' or 'the princes' as the only identifier.
rule.good_example: In-frame: Character A, screen-left, standing, facing the dais; Character B, screen-right, standing, facing A.
rule.bad_example: The prompt says 'the princes stand together' with no sides, no names, and no facing.

rule.rule_text: The rendered location must match the named location reference asset exactly, used as the background plate. Do not invent a new layout and do not mix conflicting location refs in the same shot.
rule.rationale: Conflicting plates look like a location jump even when the story is continuous.
rule.good_example: All corridor shots use the same broken-corridor front plate as the background; a second corridor tile is marked 'do not use as background'.
rule.bad_example: A shot set in a damaged interior cuts to a clean gilded hall or a moonlit exterior arch because a second location tile was allowed to become the plate.

rule.rule_text: Characters keep their established walking or travel direction. A camera or VIEW change must not make them appear to turn around or reverse direction unless the story shows that turn on screen.
rule.rationale: View labels are useful, but an unplanned reverse view is a common cause of apparent turn-backs.
rule.good_example: A character walks toward an opening; every later shot stays frontal, camera ahead, tracking back, still traveling toward that opening.
rule.bad_example: A mid-clip REVERSE view is introduced so the same walk reads as a 180-degree U-turn.

rule.rule_text: Once something breaks, tears, cracks, burns, or is otherwise damaged, it stays damaged in every later track and episode until a later approved story beat repairs or replaces it. Nothing is silently cleaned, healed, or restored.
rule.good_example: A toppled pillar, a torn banner, a scarred wrist and a cracked floor are restated as still broken in the next prompt's locks and negatives ('never stands again', 'never repaired').
rule.bad_example: A later track opens in a freshly cleaned hall, or a character's wound and torn costume have vanished with no story beat.

rule.rule_text: No eye glow. Everyone has natural, realistic eyes with real catchlights only. Allowed body glows (for example a wrist brand) stay on that body part and never reach the eyes. Do not invent an exception; only use one if the director has explicitly approved it for that beat.
rule.good_example: A close-up describes normal eyes with natural catchlights, and a wrist mark is locked to the wrist only.
rule.bad_example: A close-up gives a character yellow-orange glowing eyes, or a prompt says 'eyes burning' in a way that the model renders as luminous irises.

rule.rule_text: Continuity fixes must be written inside the relevant shot text (action, in-frame, positions, negatives that belong to that shot). Do not append override notes at the end of the prompt and expect the model to apply them.
rule.rationale: Override notes at the tail are ignored by the generator; the shot body is what gets rendered.
rule.good_example: When a character must not cry, the shot's action line says 'She does NOT cry: no tears, dry eyes and dry cheeks' and the negatives repeat it.
rule.bad_example: A paragraph added after the last shot says 'NOTE: make her stop crying and fix the walk' while the shot text still describes tears.

rule.rule_text: QC every generation before it is treated as the new continuity source. Update the continuity master from what was actually rendered, not only from the planned prompt. Label facts taken only from a prompt as unverified.
rule.good_example: After a take is approved, a reviewer checks positions, plates, damage, costume, props, eye glow, dialogue and shot structure, then writes the end state from the last frame.
rule.bad_example: The next prompt is written from the previous prompt's planned end state even though the selected render put people on the wrong sides.

rule.rule_text: A new track opens on the previous approved track's end state: positions, facing, costume, props, injuries, damage, lighting and location plate. Only the new story beats should move those facts, and the move must be visible on screen.
rule.good_example: Track 4 opens on the fallen pose from the end of track 3 and shows the character standing up; everything else is unchanged.
rule.bad_example: Track 4 opens with the character already standing in a new spot, healed, in a clean costume, as if the previous ending never happened.

rule.rule_text: Each character's wardrobe and hair must match the locked look and the assigned reference asset. Do not swap costumes between characters and do not let outfits drift mid-episode.
rule.good_example: The prompt names the exact garments from the character lock and the same reference tile in every shot.
rule.bad_example: A character who should wear a blue coat and a silver-gold breastplate is rendered all in red, or two leads swap capes mid-clip.

rule.rule_text: Exactly one instance of each unique lead appears in any frame. Never chip two different tiles of the same person as two bodies. Presence must be locked so a lead is not silently replaced or duplicated.
rule.good_example: A presence lock says the named lead is clearly visible once in every shot, and extra appearance tiles are marked 'same person, appearance reference only'.
rule.bad_example: Two copies of the same prince appear in one wide shot, or a look-alike in the crowd wears the lead's unique armour.

rule.rule_text: Lighting and grade stay consistent with the locked lighting reference for that location. Do not change lighting between shots unless the story shows a light source changing.
rule.good_example: A dark hall tile is the primary lighting and grade reference; brighter architecture tiles are used for layout only.
rule.bad_example: Shots in the same continuous scene flip from warm practicals to cool moonlight or a hard god-ray through a new hole in the roof.

rule.rule_text: Unless the director asks for score, audio is dialogue plus diegetic sound only. Do not add background music, songs, or chanted melody. Avoid musical wording ('chant swells', 'melodic hum') that the generator treats as score.
rule.good_example: The audio line lists only spoken lines and diegetic SFX (footsteps, doors, fire, crowd shouts).
rule.bad_example: A clip that should be dialogue and SFX only is covered by a loud orchestral score or a continuous drone.

rule.rule_text: Prop placement and condition are locked until a visible action moves them. A prop does not pop into a hand, change open/closed state, or relocate between shots without being handled on screen.
rule.good_example: The sheathed sword lies flat on the floor at a named spot until the scripted pickup: stop, crouch, both hands on the hilt, pull free, straighten. A book that was closed stays closed.
rule.bad_example: A sword is planted upright in the floor or appears in a hand mid-shot; a book flips from open to closed; a scabbard that should be empty shows a hilt again.

rule.rule_text: Posture words must match the blocking. If people are standing, do not also describe them as slumped, lying, or rising except in the shot where that change happens. If they are fallen, say so in every shot until they get up on camera.
rule.good_example: Guards are fallen in shots 1–2; shot 3 is the only shot in which they stand up; later shots describe them standing.
rule.bad_example: A spatial-facts line says the guards are standing, but a leftover negative says 'no one getting up' and a shot still calls them slumped.

rule.rule_text: Reference chips may point only to tiles that already exist on the card. Do not invent assets, do not use a '?' chip, and do not renumber tiles. Unused tiles stay in the list marked unused.
rule.good_example: A superseded location tile is labeled UNUSED and is not used as a background; the highest chip number is within the tile count.
rule.bad_example: The prompt chips a tile that is not on the card, or renumbers remaining tiles after one is removed, breaking later chip maps.

rule.rule_text: Label every shot with its camera view (for example FRONT or REVERSE) and make the camera line match that view. Use a reverse or opposing view only when it is approved for that shot, and check that it does not flip screen sides or walking direction.
rule.good_example: FRONT shots look toward the established background landmark; a single approved REVERSE shot is labeled and keeps character sides consistent in world space.
rule.bad_example: Unlabeled cameras wander; a sudden reverse view mirrors everyone or makes a walk look like a turn-back.

rule.rule_text: Only the speaking character's mouth moves on their line; everyone else keeps their mouth closed. Lip-sync the speaker to the verbatim line.
rule.good_example: A two-shot names the speaker, describes that mouth moving, and states that the silent character's mouth stays closed.
rule.bad_example: A silent character lip-syncs someone else's line, or the speaker's mouth stays shut while the line is heard.

rule.rule_text: Characters look at the person or object they are talking to or reacting to. Eyelines must match the locked geography.
rule.good_example: A guard on a landing looks down and toward the prince he addresses; the prince looks back and up at the guards.
rule.bad_example: The speaker looks into the lens or past the person they are addressing, while the addressee stares straight ahead and ignores them.

rule.rule_text: People who belong in the scene but are out of frame are written as behind the camera (heard, not seen), never silently dropped. If a later shot should show them, they return on the same locked sides.
rule.good_example: A close-up says the second lead is off-frame at the locked dais position (heard). The following wide puts that person back in the same spot.
rule.bad_example: A close-up of one lead simply omits the person who was standing beside them, and the next wide never brings them back.

rule.rule_text: Add negatives for every flagged failure, but delete stale negatives that contradict the new blocking. Contradictory negatives are themselves a continuity failure.
rule.good_example: After guards are required to stand up in shot 1, the old negative 'no one getting up' is removed, and a new negative forbids them sitting later.
rule.bad_example: The action says a character must walk to the gate, but a leftover negative still says no one leaves their mark.

rule.rule_text: Start from the previous end state, but do not force a 'match the last frame exactly' opening shot unless the director asks for that.
rule.rationale: One recorded case rejected a forced exact last-frame start even though continuity of positions was still required.
rule.good_example: The new track inherits positions and costume from the last approved frame, then begins the new camera move the script calls for.
rule.bad_example: The first shot is rewritten as a still hold of the previous last frame even after the director rejected that approach.

rule.rule_text: Camera may look either way along a hall, but character world positions and established screen-side locks do not flip unless the director rewrites the axis. If a reverse view is used, restate world positions so the same person is not mirrored to the opposite side.
rule.good_example: A is at the stair base on the throne-right side in every view; the prompt restates that world position in both FRONT and REVERSE.
rule.bad_example: A reverse camera is introduced and A, who was screen-right, is now written as screen-left with no story move, flipping the axis.

rule.rule_text: Time of day and key light follow the location plate and the established scene, not a conflicting second plate. Do not relight a continuous interior with a different time of day.
rule.good_example: An interior locked to warm practicals keeps those practicals in every shot; a daylight exterior plate is used only if the shot is actually exterior.
rule.bad_example: A night interior suddenly has daylight windows as the key, or a beach floor appears inside a stone fort scene.

rule.rule_text: Keep clean anatomy and unique props: one body, two hands, five fingers, one of each named weapon. Flag fused fingers, extra limbs, and duplicated blades as continuity/QC failures.
rule.rationale: These are generation artifacts, but they are recorded and fixed in the same QC pass as continuity errors.
rule.good_example: A grip is described as five clean fingers on a single named sword.
rule.bad_example: A character grows a third arm, fingers fuse into a hilt, or two blades occupy the same scabbard.

rule.rule_text: Action should read as live-action and physically weighted: real footwork, impact, and muscle work. People do not glide, float, or freeze mid-air unless the shot explicitly calls for a stylized beat the director approved.
rule.good_example: A strike is written with weight shift, impact recoil, and real-time timing; 'Muscle work:' is included in the action line.
rule.bad_example: Fighters slide like cutouts, a leaping body freezes in the air, or a character glides down stairs.

rule.rule_text: When the director requires a hard first-frame match, the opening frame must show the locked handoff pose, props and background from the previous end or a named continuity-master still. Then the new action begins.
rule.good_example: The first second holds the locked two-handed grip, background landmarks and fallen or standing poses from the continuity master before the new line starts.
rule.bad_example: The clip opens on a closer or higher angle with a different grip and missing background landmarks, so it does not cut from the previous track.
